name: Simmons SDS-V
originalPurpose: An early fully electronic drum kit from Simmons in St Albans, England. You hit hexagonal pads with ordinary sticks, and a rack of analogue circuits produced the drum sounds.
whatActuallyHappened: Its pitch-bending electronic toms became one of the signature sounds of 1980s pop. In reggae, Sly Dunbar was one of very few drummers who welcomed the new machines when most Jamaican drummers were wary of them. He used Simmons drums on Black Uhuru's 'Anthem', and his early use of electronic drums pointed toward the fully computerised dancehall that followed. Simmons replaced the SDS-V with newer models in 1983.
priceStory: Expensive new, and aimed at professional drummers. The pads were made of very hard plastic, which drummers complained hurt their wrists. For a Kingston rhythm section, the cost and the novelty are part of why Sly's adoption stood out.
hook: Hexagonal electronic drums that a Jamaican drummer took up while most others were still suspicious of them.
blurb: You play them with sticks like normal drums, but the sound comes from electronics, and the toms can swoop down in pitch like a laser. Lots of 1980s pop used them. Sly Dunbar has said in interviews, including a Red Bull Music Academy lecture, that most Jamaican drummers were afraid of drum machines while he found them fascinating, and that he used Simmons drums on Black Uhuru's album 'Anthem'. The idea that his curiosity helped point reggae toward the computer-made dancehall music that came next is a reasonable reading of the dates rather than a documented chain of cause, and the map treats it that way.
